Abanico Formation
Oligocene – early Miocene (~34 to 20 million years ago)
Volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks —mostly tuffs— that piled up in a sinking basin while an arc of volcanoes erupted. They make up most of San Cristóbal hill.
Hypabyssal intrusives
Miocene (~20 to 15 million years ago)
Magma that rose and cooled at shallow depth inside the Abanico tuffs, without reaching the surface. It forms fine- to medium-grained rocks such as microdiorite.
Unconsolidated deposits
Quaternary (last 2.6 million years)
Soil, gravel and loose sediment covering the rock on the slopes and on the Santiago plain.

A 4-metre rock face cut by fractures in every direction: the instruction manual for a rockfall.
Andesitic lapilli tuff of the Abanico Formation. Subvertical rock face 4 metres high with multidirectional fractures that create wedges with planes favourable for block sliding.
Look for fracture planes that cross each other: where two or three meet, a loose wedge of rock is left.
The fallen blocks at the foot of the slope prove that the process is still active.
Rainwater and roots push inside the fractures and slowly pry them open.
Look at the base of the slope. Every block piled up there was once wedged higher up.

Weathering and soil
The rock still keeps its fractures, but it crumbles in your hand: this is where soil is born.

Weathered and decomposed rock that still preserves its fractures. These range from open to sealed, with gypsum coatings and probably clays and minor carbonates. Trees take advantage of the weak ground and the space left by the fractures to grow their root systems.
The rock keeps the "pattern" of its fractures even though it is already decomposed: it is a ghost rock.
The white coatings in the fractures are gypsum and carbonates deposited by water.
Roots follow the fractures and speed up the breakdown of the rock.
Compare the rock next to a tree with the rock in a bare spot: vegetation changes the pace.

Microdioritic intrusion with porphyritic texture and 1–5 mm phenocrysts of plagioclase (40%) with pervasive alteration to clays, and euhedral pyroxene (10%) from 1 mm to 1.2 cm. Highly altered microcrystalline groundmass with plagioclase microlites and probable magnetite microlites (weak magnetism).
The large crystals (phenocrysts) grew slowly, at depth, inside the magma.
The fine mass around them cooled quickly when the magma rose: porphyritic texture.
The dark, shiny crystals with flat faces are pyroxene; the whitish ones, plagioclase.
Look closely at a fresh surface: the pyroxenes reflect light like tiny mirrors.

Spheroidal weathering

Microdioritic intrusion with porphyritic texture and clear concentric exfoliation structures produced by weathering of the rock.
Water attacks the rock along the fractures, which form a network of cube-shaped blocks.
The corners of each block are attacked from three sides at once, so they round off first.
The result is concentric shells around a core that is still sound.

Andesitic welded tuff of the Abanico Formation with fiamme structures up to 17.5 cm long and up to 2.5 cm thick. The fiamme are oriented between N20°W and N10°W and dip between 22° and 35° to the NE.
Fiamme are pumice fragments flattened by the weight of the hot deposit itself.
Their flattened shape defines a plane: it tells us how the unit was laid down.
Here that plane dips between 22° and 35° to the northeast.
The fiamme are parallel to each other. That shared orientation is a structural measurement.

The rock in the Tupahue pool
The rock that changed the architect's plan
Crystal ash tuff
Fracturing, texture and colour of the volcanic rock
Recreational
National Monument, Typical Zone category
It turned up at the bottom of a quarry and was so beautiful that the pool was redesigned to keep it inside.

The rocks in the pool are a crystal ash tuff of the Abanico Formation. It contains some lithic fragments and flattened pumice, which indicates some degree of welding. Its colour is violet-grey to reddish, given by an aphanitic matrix holding plagioclase crystals up to 3 mm and, less often, lithic fragments up to 15 mm.

The Tupahue pool was designed on site and originally did not include the rock. It was added after the ground was cleared of material moved by the quarry works and the rock was found at the bottom. Because of its size and beauty, the design was changed to include it.
The flat faces of the block are not quarry cuts: they are natural fault and fracture planes.
The main planes have an average strike of N30°W and are subvertical.
It is a strong rock (class R4): it withstands 50 to 100 MPa of compression.
On some faces you can still see striations: marks left by the fault movement.

The rock is split into two blocks. The flat faces are fractures, some with worn but recognizable indicators of the direction of movement. Conjugate fractures create wedges up to 1 metre that, because of how open they are, could break off into the pool.
Class R4 (Brown, 1981): takes 2 to 3 hammer blows to break; estimated uniaxial compressive strength between 50 and 100 MPa.

Columns of intrusive rock on Av. Pedro Bannen
The magma cracked as it cooled
Cooling structures in hypabyssal rocks
Columns 5 or 6 metres long with 4- to 6-sided faces, growing perpendicular to the contact with the cold rock.

Microdioritic intrusion with porphyritic texture, with plagioclase crystals (60%) of 0.1–2 mm, amphibole (7%) averaging 1 mm and opaques (probably magnetite, 5%). The rock is strongly magnetic.

Columnar jointing is visible, with columns about 5 to 6 m long and 0.3 m in average diameter, with basal faces of 4 to 6 sides. The columns occur near the contact between the volcanic rock and the intrusion, and they form as the magma cools close to the contact with the cold volcanic rock. The columns grow perpendicular to the contact zone, and the fractures spread from the contact into the magma as it cools.
As it cools, the magma shrinks and cracks into polygons, just like drying mud.
Each polygon extends downwards and forms a column.
The columns grow perpendicular to the cooling surface, so they point towards the contact.
Count the sides of a basal face: they are almost always 5 or 6. The rock is magnetic; a compass may swing near it.

Rock of pyroclastic origin, with lithics and broken crystals, mainly plagioclase, altered to clay. Highly fractured and weathered outcrop. Subvertical N34°W fracture plane with striations of rake 2.9°.
Striations are parallel scratches carved when the blocks rubbed against each other.
A rake of almost 0° means almost horizontal movement: a strike-slip fault.
The plane strikes N34°W and is subvertical.
Hold your phone's light low across the surface: the striations suddenly appear.

Weakly porphyritic texture. Phenocrysts averaging 1 mm: plagioclase (20%), amphibole (10%) and opaques, probably magnetite (5%), with oxidation rims. Equigranular microcrystalline groundmass.
Dark greenish-grey on the outer surface and light greenish-grey on a fresh surface.
The fractures hold white layers of calcite deposited by circulating water.
It is a very dense and strong rock.
Compare the colour of an exposed face with a freshly broken one: it is the same rock.
Dark greenish-grey on the outer surface, locally with white layers of calcite; light greenish-grey on a fresh surface.
Intrusive rocks on the summit of San Cristóbal
The roof of the park, on intrusive rock
Intrusive rock on the summit
Educational / scenic
The summit stays high because it is made of the hardest rock on the hill: the intrusion.

Porphyritic texture with 1–5 mm phenocrysts of plagioclase (40%) with pervasive alteration to clays, and euhedral pyroxene (10%) from 1 mm to 1.2 cm. Highly altered microcrystalline groundmass with plagioclase microlites and probable magnetite microlites (weak magnetism).
The intrusion resists erosion better than the tuffs: that is why it forms the summits.
From here you can see the Santiago basin, filled with sediment, and the mountain front of the Andes.
It is the same microdiorite as in geosites 4, 5, 9 and 12: one single body, several windows.
Look east: the change in slope marks the edge of the Santiago basin.
El Hundimiento viewpoint
Viewpoint used to explain the landforms of Santiago and the geological history of the region: the sediment-filled basin, the chain of island hills and the Andes in the background.
El Hundimiento quarry

Old quarry. The rock is completely weathered and altered to clays and calcite, and there is evidence of a possible fault zone: the left half of the face is pale yellow. Unstable slopes: view it from the path.

34 to 20 million years ago
Volcanoes and a sinking basin
An arc of volcanoes erupts while the ground sinks. Ash, pumice and lava pile up layer upon layer: this is the Abanico Formation, the rock of most of the hill.
About 20 to 15 million years ago
Magma that never made it out
Bodies of magma rise and stall at shallow depth inside the tuffs. As they cool they form the microdiorite, and at their cold edges they crack into columns.
Since then
The Andes rise and the hill is left isolated
Tectonic shortening lifts the Andes and deforms these rocks. Faults and fractures form, and their striations can still be read on the hill.
Last 2.6 million years
The basin fills up
Rivers fill the Santiago basin with sediment. The San Cristóbal ridge is left as an island hill rising above the fill.
Today
The rock keeps falling apart
Water, roots and temperature changes break down the rock, create soil and loosen blocks from the slopes. The whole process can be seen at the geosites in this park.
